taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes it is composed of two groups formerly considered separate species, quiscula (Purple Grackle) and versicolor (Bronzed Grackle); studies disagree on whether they are conspecific.
fieldMarks: Male glossy black with an iridescent bluish or purplish head, neck and breast; female less glossy
Long tail with a crease down the middle, whitish-yellow eyes, strong bill; 28-34 cm
Bronzed form: bronzy body contrasts with blue-black head; Purple form of the southeast has purple and green gloss with less contrast
Juveniles have dark eyes; molting birds in late summer have short or ragged tails
behavior: Migrates in flocks by day; partial migrant, present all year in much of the eastern U.S.
Forages walking or wading, also up in trees and shrubs, usually in flocks when not nesting; sometimes steals food from other birds
Omnivorous: mostly grains and seeds in winter and migration, insects in summer, also crayfish, minnows, frogs, eggs and young of other birds
Nests and roosts in dense trees, especially conifers, near open areas
habitat: Open or semi-open country: farmland, towns, groves and streamsides; forages in farm fields, pastures, suburban lawns, feedlots and marshes.
range: Breeds from northeastern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida, west to Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico; winters from Kansas, the southern Great Lakes and New England south.

lookalikes.name: Great-tailed grackle
lookalikes.howToTell: Larger with a much longer tail and more evenly coloured male.

lookalikes.name: Rusty blackbird
lookalikes.howToTell: Smaller, with a shorter tail and thinner bill.
